name: Orthodontic extractions debate

lead: Orthodontic choices shape both the smile and the facial profile, which is why looksmaxxers follow this debate. Orthodontists sometimes remove teeth, most often premolars, to relieve crowding or change the lip profile, and the question of whether to has been argued since the early 1900s.

Mainstream orthodontics treats extraction as one option chosen case by case, based on crowding, bite and profile. Orthotropic proponents, following John Mew, regard extractions as potentially harmful to facial growth and favour expansion; the orthotropic view is not supported by mainstream professional bodies. In looksmaxxing circles the argument is usually framed around the claim that extractions shrink the jaws and flatten the face, and published evidence on this is limited and contested.

paras: People weigh the options in consultations: extraction plans create space so remaining teeth can be aligned or retracted, while non-extraction plans such as expansion make room another way. Many seek second opinions before choosing.
Extractions are irreversible and carry general surgical risks. Non-extraction plans such as expansion also have limits and relapse risk. Community members often describe fear of a changed profile.

chain: Change in tooth alignment and profile
angle.text: Looksmaxxers follow this debate because orthodontic choices shape both the smile and the facial profile. Premolar removal or arch expansion changes tooth alignment and how the profile sits. One camp holds extractions flatten the face and favours expansion, while orthodontic history shows both approaches in use.

lead: The orthodontic extractions debate concerns whether teeth, usually premolars, should be removed to resolve crowding and improve the facial profile, or whether space should instead be created by other means such as arch expansion. It is one of the oldest disputes in orthodontics. Edward Angle and his followers strongly opposed extraction and believed ideal occlusion would also yield good facial aesthetics, while Charles Tweed and Raymond Begg reintroduced extraction in the 1940s and 1950s to improve aesthetics and the stability of results [1]. Teeth are reportedly extracted in about half of cases today, most commonly premolars [1].

In looksmaxxing communities the topic is tied to orthotropics, a system founded by British orthodontist John Mew that argues malocclusion is largely environmental and postural. Mew held that extractions, fixed appliances with elastics and retractive headgear could harm facial growth [2]. Mainstream professional orthodontists do not support orthotropics, and commentators have described the evidence for it as inadequate [2].
infobox: Angle versus Tweed and Begg, early to mid 20th century [1]

paras: Angle, described as the father of modern orthodontics, prioritised perfect occlusion and opposed extractions. Earlier figures such as Norman Kingsley often removed teeth for crowding without much attention to occlusal relationships [1].

Focusing on occlusion alone was later seen as neglecting facial proportions, since even ideal occlusion was not always aesthetically satisfying. Cephalometric radiographs also showed that many Class II and Class III malocclusions arise from jaw relationships rather than tooth position alone [1]. Tweed and Begg, both Angle's students, returned to extraction partly for these reasons [1].

Mew argued that conventional orthodontics straightens teeth without addressing the underlying cause of crowding, and concluded that extractions could be harmful to facial growth. He also held that malocclusion is postural and environmental rather than mainly genetic [2]. Orthotropic methods include palatal expanders, dietary changes and a specific resting tongue position, and the associated do-it-yourself technique, mewing, gained wide social media attention from 2019 [2].

Mew faced disciplinary action from the UK General Dental Council, including a reprimand in 2010 over advertising and revocation of his licence in 2017 [2]. Reviewers have described parts of his theory as plausible but the evidence for efficacy as inadequate [2].

The Wikipedia overview of orthodontics states that conclusive scientific evidence for the health benefits of orthodontic treatment is lacking, though patients who complete treatment report higher quality of life than untreated patients awaiting treatment [1]. It describes extraction as a continuing standard option rather than a default.

Palatal expansion is accepted in orthodontics as a way to create space, with fixed tissue-borne appliances considered the best approach for maxillary expansion and removable expanders mainly tipping teeth outward. Proper expansion can create space and may improve oral and nasal airflow [1].

No studies found specifically testing the claim, made in orthotropic circles, that premolar extractions impair facial growth. General reviews of orthodontics note that evidence on the long-term effect of treatment choices on facial appearance is limited [1].

Anti-extraction advice circulates alongside mewing, maxilla expansion and jaw-growth discussion. Members commonly describe wanting to avoid extractions in the belief that retained teeth preserve a forward midface. Orthodontists and the cited overview describe the choice as dependent on the individual's crowding, skeletal pattern and profile [1].

lore.intro: In forums, extractions are often presented as a decision that can permanently narrow the face, and avoiding them is bundled with orthotropic practices.

claims.claim: Extractions shrink the arches and flatten the face.
Crowding can be solved by expansion instead of extraction.

timeline.event: Tweed and Begg reintroduce extraction to orthodontic practice [1].
John Mew is reprimanded by the General Dental Council over advertising [2].
Mew's licence is revoked by the General Dental Council [2].
Mewing reaches wide social media and mainstream attention [2].
